You compare people, places and things (più grande di, meno caro che, tanto quanto) and use the superlative (il più bello, bellissimo) and the irregular forms migliore, meglio, peggiore, peggio.
This flat is bigger than the other one.
Florence is less chaotic than Naples.
Neapolitan pizza is the best in the world.
Giulia cooks better than I do.
To compare with più… di / meno… di: Giulia è più alta di Pietro.
To use "che" instead of "di" when comparing two adjectives, verbs or quantities.
To express equality: (tanto)… quanto, così… come.
To form the relative superlative: il più bello della città.
To form the absolute superlative: bellissimo, molto bello, stanchissima.
To use the irregular forms: migliore / meglio, peggiore / peggio, maggiore / minore.
April. Giulia's landlord is selling the flat on via dei Serragli, so Giulia has to move. On Saturday morning she sees two flats with Matei and an estate agent, Signor Rinaldi.
So, this is the first one: sixty square metres, third floor, near Santa Croce.
It's bigger than my flat now. And much brighter!
Yes, but the street is incredibly noisy. There are more scooters than people.
It's the centre, sir. The rent is nine hundred euros a month.
Nine hundred?! That's more expensive than a castle!
Then let's go and see the second one. It's in the Oltrarno, on via della Chiesa.
In the Oltrarno? Five minutes from Graziella's trattoria!
Here we are. It's smaller than the first, only forty-five square metres, but it's very quiet. And there's a little terrace.
Oh, what a view! You can see the rooftops and the dome of the Duomo!
Six hundred and fifty euros. It's the best-value flat in the neighbourhood.
It's smaller, but it's much nicer. And it costs less. It's perfect!
And above all it's closer to me than to the workshop.
That's the best advantage of all!
The stress falls on "IS", with a double S: bel-LIS-si-mo, tran-quil-LIS-si-mo, bwo-NIS-si-mo.
GG + i + o = a long "j": PEG-gio = "ped-jo".
PIÙ (more) and MENO (less) + adjective + DI (than). "Di" merges with the article: del, della, dei…
Giulia è più alta di Pietro.
Firenze è meno grande di Roma.
Il primo appartamento è più caro del secondo.
The first flat is more expensive than the second.
Matei è più timido di me.
After "di" come the stressed pronouns: di me, di te, di lui, di lei, di noi, di voi, di loro.
Use DI when comparing two people or things (nouns, pronouns). Use CHE when comparing two adjectives, two verbs, two quantities or two phrases with prepositions:
È più bello che comodo. (More beautiful than comfortable.)
Mi piace più leggere che scrivere.
Ci sono più motorini che persone.
È più vicino a me che al laboratorio.
Quick rule: if "than" is followed directly by a noun or pronoun → DI. Otherwise → CHE.
Pietro is as lively as his grandmother.
Sibiu is as beautiful as Florence.
I have as many books as paintings.
"Tanto" and "così" can be left out: "È alto quanto me" = "He's as tall as me".
The RELATIVE superlative (the most… in): article + più / meno + adjective + DI. The ABSOLUTE superlative (very…): adjective minus its last vowel + -ISSIMO.
il ponte più famoso di Firenze
la ragazza più simpatica della classe
Watch the spelling: lungo → lunghissimo, ricco → ricchissimo (with H, to keep the sound). Simpatico → simpaticissimo.
In Romanian: "cel mai frumos pod" — in Italian the article goes with the noun: "IL ponte più bello", not "il più bello ponte".
The classic mistake: MIGLIORE is an adjective (un vino migliore), MEGLIO is an adverb (canta meglio). Never "più meglio"! "Mio fratello maggiore" = my older brother.
Is the Duomo taller than the bell tower?
Pietro is as tall as his cousin.
It's the most famous bridge in Florence.

Ci sono più motorini di persone.
Ci sono più motorini delle persone.

On the Monday after Easter, Pasquetta, Italians have a picnic. Graziella closed the trattoria and packed an enormous basket: sandwiches, frittata, salami, colomba and two bottles of wine. Together they all climbed the hill of Fiesole: Graziella, Pietro, Matei, Giulia and even Signor Franco.
From up there Florence was beautiful: the red rooftops, the dome, the river shining in the sun. "It's the most beautiful city in the world," said Graziella, with her mouth full of frittata.
Giulia raised an eyebrow. "More beautiful than Naples? Naples has the sea, Vesuvius, the sun. Naples is livelier, happier and warmer than Florence."
"Warmer, yes," Graziella replied. "And also more chaotic, noisier and dirtier. In Florence we have Michelangelo, Botticelli, Brunelleschi. The Renaissance was born here, my dear."

So the great contest began. Is Neapolitan pizza better than Florentine schiacciata? Is Naples coffee stronger? Are Neapolitans friendlier than Florentines? Do Florentines speak Italian better than anyone? Every question was a battle.
Signor Franco, who was the oldest, was the referee. He gave a point to Naples, a point to Florence, and drank a glass of wine for every point. After an hour he was the happiest of them all.
In the end Giulia turned to Matei. "And you? Which is the most beautiful city, in your opinion?" Graziella was looking at him too. Matei was in danger: any answer was the worst.
He thought for a moment. "For me the most beautiful city is Sibiu," he said. "It's smaller than Florence and colder than Naples. But my mother, my father and my sister are there."
Graziella and Giulia looked at each other. "Clever," said Graziella. "Very clever," said Giulia. And they both laughed.

But the final verdict was given by Pietro, who until then had silently eaten the whole colomba. "You're all wrong," he said. "The most beautiful city is the one with the best ice cream. And the best ice cream in the world is the pistachio one near the bridge. So Florence wins."
Nobody could reply. It was the strongest argument of the day.
